<<12:27 notes, part 0 of 0..1>>
[MUQATIL:12:27-31/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A tear from behind means Joseph fled from her, so the woman lied and Joseph spoke truthfully.
[MUQATIL:12:27-31/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | They heard the pair's commotion and the shirt tearing behind the door.
[TAB-FULL:v13p101/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says the husband was seated at the door with the woman's cousin; she accused Joseph, Joseph countered that she had pursued him, and the cousin proposed judging by the shirt, which was torn from behind.
[TAB-FULL:v13p104/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Joseph answers that he did not solicit her; she solicited him, and he is defending himself against her accusation.
[TAB-FULL:v13p104/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نوف الشامي | reports | Nawf al-Shami says Joseph had not meant to mention her conduct until she accused him; then he became angry and answered that she had pursued him.
[TAB-FULL:v13p111#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The shirt's direction settles the dispute: a fugitive is struck from behind, while a tear at the front would indicate that Joseph pursued and was lying.
[TAB-FULL:v13p111#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the shirt itself adjudicated between the two.
[TAB-FULL:v13p112/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The particle أن is omitted before the witness's if-clause because the testimony is construed as speech, as though someone from her family said it.
[TAB-FULL:v13p112/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari compares the ellipsis with the inheritance statement in 4:11, which is likewise construed as speech. | mentions 4:11
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2129#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عامر | reports | ʿAmir says Joseph’s shirt had three signs: its back was torn, it later restored his father’s sight, and its false blood showed the wolf had not eaten him because it would have torn the shirt. | mentions 12:18, 12:93
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2129#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | A wise family witness proposes the shirt as evidence: a front tear would mean the woman spoke truth and Joseph lied.
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2129#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · محمد بن اسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq says the witness was a trusted man from Qitfir’s family; he reasoned that a man approaches a woman from the front, not from behind, so the tear proves Joseph’s account.
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2129#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says her cousin proposed that a front tear would prove her truth and Joseph’s lie, while a back tear would prove the opposite; the shirt was torn from behind.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | Abu Jaafar finds it likeliest that the witness was a wise adult whom the king consulted.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | A child's testimony for Joseph would itself be a clearer miracle than inference from the shirt.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The hadith of four who spoke as infants is compatible: Joseph's witness could be young without being a small child.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن عباس | reports | Abu Jaafar says Ibn Abbas repeatedly transmitted that Joseph's witness was not a child.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | إن كان قميصه is conditional and jussive, though conditionals normally project past verbs into the future.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · المازني | reports | Al-Mazini explains the past-tense form by positing an omitted القول.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · محمد بن يزيد | reports | Muhammad ibn Yazid says كان is broad enough to express all actions.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r21] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq explains إن كان as إن يعلم: knowing has not yet occurred, and كان can express that meaning.
[NAHHAS:v2p323/r22] NAHHAS, d. 338 · زهير | reports | Abu Ishaq cites a line by Zuhayr as a parallel for expressing this meaning with a past form.
[NAHHAS:v2p325/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Zuhayr's line is cited as a parallel for the past-tense conditional construction.
[NAHHAS:v2p325/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · يحيى بن يعمر وابن أبي إسحاق | reports | These readers use ḍamma on qāf, bāʾ, and lām in قد من قبل; they do likewise with دبر.
[NAHHAS:v2p325/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq treats من قبل and من دبر as endpoints, and permits fatḥa in both.
[THALABI:v5p215/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid identifies the witness as the shirt torn from behind; the witness is a judge who says the shirt will clarify the matter.
[THALABI:v5p215/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Ibn Abī Isḥāq softens “qubul” and “dubur”; the other readers intensify them, two dialects.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p27/r15] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | A front tear would show Joseph had approached her; a back tear would show he was fleeing from her.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p27/r16] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Joseph's shirt is one of three signs: its back tear proved him truthful, the false blood on it exposed his brothers, and its placement on Jacob's face restored his sight. | mentions 12:18, 12:96
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p84/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The witness’s test and explanation use the shirt’s front or back tear to distinguish the truthful party from the liar.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:27-30/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | A tear in the back means the woman lied and Joseph told the truth.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p236#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Jurists who allow judgment from circumstantial signs rely on this verse’s shirt evidence.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p236/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Most read “in front” and “behind” with ḍamma and tanwīn; another reading builds them as adverbs, which Abū Ḥātim calls very poor Arabic. Other readers report forms with still bāʾ or unmarked endings.
[TABRISI:12:25-28/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن يعمر وابن أبي إسحاق ونوح القارئ | reports | These readers anomalously pronounce min qabl and min dubur with three dammas and no tanwin.
[TABRISI:12:25-28/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Min in 'from behind/from in front' marks the tear's starting point; min in 'among the liars' is partitive.
[TABRISI:12:25-28/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinni treats these as terminal adverbs after deletion of the pronoun, like the verse 'before and after.' | mentions 30:4
[TABRISI:12:25-29/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A front tear would support her claim and make Joseph the aggressor; a back tear proves the reverse because he fled and she pursued.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:26-28/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read qabl and dubr as terminal adverbs with suppressed possessors; other readers use diptote-like fatḥa or shortened genitive forms.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:27/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | A tear from behind shows she pursued Joseph and pulled his garment; the conditional may be quoted speech or testimony treated as speech, and calling it testimony reflects its function.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:27/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The pairing إن كان can mean if it becomes known that it was so, like a conditional where past kindness is stated after a future condition.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:27/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Qiraat read min qablu and min duburu with ḍamma as fixed adverbs, fatḥa as indeclinable names of directions, or with a still middle vowel.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p185#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | If the shirt was torn behind, she lied and Joseph spoke truth; the implied syntax is that the witness said, if the shirt proves to be torn this way.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p185#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | A front tear would support her because Joseph was hurrying after her, might stumble and tear its front, or she could have torn it while pushing him away.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p185#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Indefinite qablu and duburu mean from a direction called front or back; combining future-oriented in with kāna means if it turns out his shirt was torn from behind.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p261/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read min qablu and min duburu with ḍamma on bāʾ and tanwīn; other authorities report silent bāʾ or three ḍammas.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p261/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حاتم والزمخشري | reports | Abū Ḥātim calls the built form poor Arabic; al-Zamakhsharī explains the terms as the shirt’s front and back.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p262#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The clauses parallel the saying that whoever obeys God and His Messenger is rightly guided, while whoever disobeys goes astray.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p262/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The continuation reports Ibn Abī Isḥāq’s fatḥ reading and treats the terms as feminine proper names for the directions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p262/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | A front tear can fit Joseph following while she pushed him away or his shirt catching as he hurried after her.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p262/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The truth and lie clauses reinforce what the condition implies; passive qadda hides who tore the shirt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p262/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Because the witness is from her family, he first makes her truth conditional on a front tear and explicitly names each independent clause’s subject.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | فكذبت and فصدقت imply قد, which brings a past verb close to the present state; a frozen verb needs no overt or understood قد.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · العامة | reports | The common reading inflects من دبر and من قبل with tanwin, meaning ‘from behind’ and ‘from in front,’ whether of the shirt or Joseph.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحسن، أبو عمرو | reports | Al-Ḥasan and a transmission from 
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

Abū ʿAmr quiesce the ʿayn as a lightening, a Hijaz and Asad dialect.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن يعمر، ابن أبي إسحاق، العطاردي، الجارود | reports | Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-ʿAṭāridī, and al-Jārūd read both words with three ḍammas; some transmissions also quiesce ʿayn and build both on ḍamma.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The ḍamma-built form analogizes to قبل and بعد when cut off from annexation, making the word itself an endpoint; the underlying forms are inflected nouns, not adverbs.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو حاتم | rejects | Abū Ḥātim calls this construction poor Arabic, since it occurs only with adverbs.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī takes the tanwin as indefinite: ‘from a side called front’ or ‘a side called back’; Ibn Abī Isḥāq also reads من قبل ومن دبر with fatḥa as feminine place names, hence diptotes.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:27/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · المبرد | reports | For كان in the conditional clause, al-Mubarrad holds that it retains its past-time meaning; another view makes it future like other verbs, in a clause serving clarification.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p383/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A rear tear supports Joseph: as he fled, she grabbed the back of his shirt to pull him toward her and tore it there.
[BURHAN:v1p415/r11] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The Aziz's wife followed desire yet failed despite worldly power; Yusuf's obedience saved him from prison and brought authority, showing happiness comes through obedience. | mentions 12:56
[BURHAN:v4p63/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The author urges attention to these verses' arrangement as part of the Qur'an's inimitability, which must be contemplated. | mentions 40:28
[BURHAN:v4p63/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The shirt test first allows the woman to be truthful and calls him a liar only indirectly; its reverse condition gently leads the opponent to the conclusion.
[NASHR:v1p233/r14] NASHR, d. 833 · بعضهم | reports | Some authorities prefer stopping after “فكذبت” in the conditional about Joseph’s shirt, then beginning “وهو من الصادقين.”
[NASHR:v1p234/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Stopping at wa-huwa mina al-ṣādiqīn signals that Joseph is truthful in his claim.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A tear from behind means she lied about Joseph and he is truthful in saying that she solicited him.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفاضل المتعقب | reports | On that account, the witness mentions the nonexistent front tear first to appear impartial, while passive wording conceals who caused the actual tear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The two conditional statements are either introduced by an implied qāla, as Basran grammarians say, or governed by shahida, as Kufans allow for reported speech.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Repeating إن in the second condition signals its independence and adds clarity; the final clauses reinforce what the preceding statements already imply.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī explains a front tear as consistent with her pushing Joseph away, or with him hurrying after her and tripping on his garment.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن المنير | rejects | Ibn al-Munīr argues that either proposed front-tear scenario could also occur when she was pursuing him; pulling is the likelier cause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author answers that the rapid encounter favors the simplest movement: if she chased him, a rear tear is the easier pull and needs no turn back.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If she pursued him and he tripped while escaping, it is natural that she would cling to him and tear the back of the shirt.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفاضل المتعقب | reports | A later critic says that if the witness was an infant, his declaration alone would prove Joseph's innocence; the shirt signs need not match the result.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p221#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفاضل المتعقب | reports | If the witness was an observing relative, he used the shirt sign to avoid publicly shaming her while relying on the known rear tear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | For the infant-witness account, the rear tear is the decisive sign and the front tear is only a setup, so no matching explanation is needed for both.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | For the wise adult witness, the nearest rationale is that a rear tear shows Joseph moving away and a front tear would show him approaching.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author doubts that shirt direction alone would satisfy a wise judge, since that inference is not certain.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن الكمال | reports | Ibn al-Kamāl says the first condition is a counterfactual foil because the witness knew the rear tear actually occurred; he criticizes al-Bayḍāwī's reading.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The witness can mention the possible front tear as though it were true to emphasize that it did not happen, just as someone can deny conveying a specific message despite speaking to its recipient.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صبغة الله الحيدري | reports | Ṣibghat Allāh al-Ḥaydarī says each tear direction fits one party's account: front if Joseph approached and she resisted, rear if she chased as he fled.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author finds no evidence that the quarrel was phrased in those terms and says a front tear would have exposed her lie immediately.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p222/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن الفرس | reports | Ibn al-Faras cites the verse for judges who may decide from circumstantial signs when formal proof is unavailable, including lost property, theft, deposits, and property boundaries.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p223/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الرازي | reports | Al-Rāzī says the earlier indications against the woman fell short of certainty, so the shirt was added as corroboration, not the sole basis of judgment.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p223/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحسن وأبو عمرو | reports | Al-Ḥasan and one transmission from Abū ʿAmr read qibal and dubur with a still bāʾ and tanwīn, a Hijazī and Asadī usage.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p223/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو يعمر وابن أبي إسحاق والعطاردي وأبو الزناد | reports | These readers pronounce qibal and dubur with three ḍammas.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p223/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حاتم | rejects | Abū Ḥātim calls the built form on ḍamma poor Arabic because these are declinable nouns, not adverbs.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p223/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq reads the two direction terms with fatḥa, apparently treating them as feminine proper names for the directions.
[ASAD-NOTES:12:24#n25/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The Qur'anic episodes in 12:26-34 are absent from Genesis, where the husband immediately believes the accusation and imprisons Joseph.
[ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them. | mentions 2:216
[BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p398/r2] BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · author | holds | The Qur’anic form qidada is unique; its root retains the basic sense of tearing, as in Joseph’s shirt torn from front or back. | mentions 72:11, 12:25, 12:28
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p161/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The wife tried to clear herself before her husband and make Joseph appear guilty; the torn shirt served as circumstantial evidence for resolving the dispute.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:26/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | A likely experienced family member arriving with the official proposed the torn-shirt test: a front tear would favor the wife, a back tear Joseph.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:26/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · Mevdûdî | reports | Maududi suggests the family witness may have been a judge, though the source says this is uncertain.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:26/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Whether or not he was a judge, the witness was just: despite belonging to the wife's family, he did not take sides.
[STUDYQURAN:12:26/r1] STUDYQURAN · Bg | reports | Joseph’s defense means that Zulaykhā sought illicit sex and he refused and fled.
[STUDYQURAN:12:26/r2] STUDYQURAN · R | reports | Many traditional sources identify the witness from her family as a wise paternal cousin.
[STUDYQURAN:12:26/r3] STUDYQURAN · Kl | reports | A shirt torn in front would support Zulaykhā’s claim, since it would suggest she defended herself from Joseph.
[STUDYQURAN:12:26/r4] STUDYQURAN · Kl | reports | A shirt torn behind supports Joseph’s truthfulness because Zulaykhā chased him and grabbed his shirt to stop him fleeing.

<<end of notes>>
